rating_evidence.coherence: The no-match heading and yellow suggested search share the left side of the panel, giving the eye a clear next step.
rating_evidence.originality: A dashed chain-saw outline on a pegboard becomes a solid folding saw when the search succeeds.
rating_evidence.craft: The hinge, teeth and pegboard fasteners make both tools recognizable. The product name has the strongest type in the result panel.
rating_evidence.usability: A visible keyboard outline moves from the suggestion to the match-count heading directly above the available tool.

primary_action.input: Three Tabs, then Enter on “Search for pruning saw”.
primary_action.expected: Replace the chain-saw empty state with one available Folding Pruning Saw.
primary_action.observed: The field changed to “pruning saw”. Focus landed on “1 match for ‘pruning saw’”, followed by one Folding Pruning Saw marked “Available”.

1A-1440.edge_observation: Manual Search also found the saw. Deleting the query left the previous result visible until submission. Submitting the blank field produced “Enter a tool name” and restored the suggestion.
1A-1440.weakness: Even after blank submission, the pegboard still depicts a missing chain saw. The illustration implies a query the user has erased.
1A-1440.repair: Show the empty-query prompt as soon as the last character is deleted. Use the bare pegboard for that state.
1A-1440.strength: The illustration explains the difference between an unavailable tool and an available alternative.

rating_evidence.coherence: The search field and Search button share one row. The full-width yellow suggestion comes before the illustration.
rating_evidence.originality: The pegboard becomes the lower half of the card, preserving the missing-tool outline and its illustrated replacement.
rating_evidence.craft: The suggested query and product name each fit on one line. The small stock count sits on a separate line beneath the button.
rating_evidence.usability: The suggestion, focused match heading, product name and checked availability badge were visible without scrolling.

primary_action.input: Three Tabs, then Enter on the yellow suggestion.
primary_action.expected: Show the available pruning saw and give the keyboard user a clear result.
primary_action.observed: The query changed to “pruning saw”. A visible outline surrounded the one-match heading above Folding Pruning Saw and its “Available” badge.

1A-390.edge_observation: Editing back to “chain saw” and activating Search restored the original no-match state. Clearing a successful query required another submission to show “Enter a tool name”.
1A-390.weakness: With the field empty, the previous product name, stock badge and large saw drawing still look like the current answer.
1A-390.repair: Replace the result card with the empty-query prompt immediately on clear, keeping focus in the field.
1A-390.strength: The phone layout gives the recovery action the full content width while keeping the tool recognizable.

rating_evidence.coherence: The joined search field and button, divider and related-search ticket align in one narrow central column.
rating_evidence.originality: The pale-green ticket uses notches and a perforated stock-count stub to connect the suggestion with inventory.
rating_evidence.craft: The suggestion has a distinct focus outline. After activation, the input border and visible clear control identify the active field.
rating_evidence.usability: Focus returns to an editable query, and the accessibility status names the tool and its availability.

primary_action.input: Three Tabs, then Enter on “Search for pruning saw”.
primary_action.expected: Run the suggested query and show the available tool.
primary_action.observed: One Folding Pruning Saw appeared with “Available”. The searchbox regained focus with “pruning saw” entered.

1B-1440.edge_observation: Escape and select-all followed by Backspace both immediately produced “Enter a search term”. The separate Search button returned the correct results for both tested queries.
1B-1440.weakness: On success, the repeated query is much larger than the product name. The user has to read past the most prominent text to identify what is available.
1B-1440.repair: Use the larger result type for Folding Pruning Saw and reduce the query to a match-count caption.
1B-1440.strength: A keyboard user can read the result and immediately revise or clear the query.

rating_evidence.coherence: The form, no-match message and suggestion fit together near the top of the viewport.
rating_evidence.originality: The notched ticket remains recognizable at phone width, and the successful result gains a small folding-saw illustration.
rating_evidence.craft: The product name fits on one line, but the stock stub breaks “1 tool available” across three lines.
rating_evidence.usability: The focused field exposes its clear control while the complete product row remains visible below.

primary_action.input: Three Tabs, then Enter on the suggested search.
primary_action.expected: Show one available Folding Pruning Saw at the same viewport size.
primary_action.observed: The product and “Available” appeared together. Focus returned to the populated searchbox, and the accessibility status confirmed the match.

1B-390.edge_observation: Activating the visible × immediately removed the result, showed “Enter a search term” and kept focus in the field. Keyboard deletion also worked. A manual “chain saw” search restored the suggestion.
1B-390.weakness: The narrow stock stub gives a single count nearly a third of the ticket and separates “tool” from “available”.
1B-390.repair: Use “1 available” on the mobile stub and give the suggested action the recovered width.
1B-390.strength: The clear control delivers immediate, visible recovery without a second submission.

rating_evidence.coherence: The ruled empty schedule ends before the explicit “Available shift” label and orange offer.
rating_evidence.originality: The taped carton, barcode and dotted print texture identify Packing at a glance.
rating_evidence.craft: The dark Reserve button has a conspicuous keyboard ring against the orange surface. The booked card keeps its alignment as it moves up.
rating_evidence.usability: One Tab reaches Reserve. The empty message disappears and a focused, checkmarked confirmation replaces the action.

primary_action.input: Tab to “Reserve shift” on Packing, Wednesday 4–6 pm, then Enter.
primary_action.expected: One booking under Upcoming shifts with an identifiable confirmation and focus target.
primary_action.observed: Exactly one Packing entry appeared under Upcoming shifts with Wednesday 4–6 pm. The reservation button disappeared. Focus moved to the outlined “Shift booked” confirmation.

2A-1440.edge_observation: A second Enter left one booking. Reload retained the booked shift.
2A-1440.weakness: The time is a small inline detail beneath “Packing”, while the parcel occupies roughly a third of the card. The scheduling decision gets less emphasis than the activity.
2A-1440.repair: Increase the size and weight of the day and time together so they can be scanned alongside the shift name.
2A-1440.strength: Moving the recognizable orange card into Upcoming shifts makes the change in ownership easy to follow.

rating_evidence.coherence: Packing, Wednesday and the time form a readable stack beside the carton, with the action spanning the row below.
rating_evidence.originality: The parcel becomes a compact illustration beside the shift details. Its packing tape and barcode survive the reduction.
rating_evidence.craft: The illustration clears the text and button. The mint success strip inherits the full width and outlined shape of the former control.
rating_evidence.usability: The entire offer fits in view. Booking moves focus to a visible confirmation directly beneath the same day and time.

primary_action.input: Tab once, then Enter on “Reserve shift”.
primary_action.expected: Move the Wednesday 4–6 pm Packing offer into Upcoming shifts once.
primary_action.observed: One Packing card appeared below Upcoming shifts. The full-width Reserve button became a focused “Shift booked” paragraph with a checkmark.

2A-390.edge_observation: Enter on the confirmation created no duplicate. Reload showed the single booked card.
2A-390.weakness: The full-width focused confirmation still looks like a button, inviting another press after the task is complete.
2A-390.repair: Focus the booked card and show a compact “Shift booked” badge beside the shift details.
2A-390.strength: The volunteer can identify the job, read the time and reach the action without scrolling past the artwork.

rating_evidence.coherence: The tinted date column, shift name and right-aligned Reserve action establish a clear reading order.
rating_evidence.originality: The divided schedule ticket gives the time a distinct place, though the green card and status pills are familiar.
rating_evidence.craft: The date divider, type alignment and whole-card focus outline keep the booked record easy to read.
rating_evidence.usability: The checked “Booked” badge appears inside the focused record, and the accessibility status reads “Shift reserved.”

primary_action.input: Tab once, then Enter on “Reserve shift” for Packing, Wednesday 4–6 pm.
primary_action.expected: One booked shift under Upcoming shifts with confirmation and visible focus.
primary_action.observed: One Packing article moved into the Upcoming shifts region. It showed Wednesday 4–6 pm and “Booked”. Focus surrounded the article, and the Reserve button disappeared.

2B-1440.edge_observation: A second Enter left one booking. The optional reload check restored “No shifts scheduled” and the available offer. Reserving again produced one booking.
2B-1440.weakness: The desktop row places Reserve far from Packing. After booking, the focus outline encloses a broad empty area to the right of the confirmation.
2B-1440.repair: Tighten the row width to bring the action closer to the shift it affects.
2B-1440.strength: The prominent time block makes it easy to decide whether the shift fits, and the focused record keeps that context after booking.

rating_evidence.coherence: Wednesday and 4–6 pm occupy the left cell, Packing and its status occupy the right, and Reserve gets a full-width row.
rating_evidence.originality: The two-column ticket preserves the relationship between time and task on a narrow screen.
rating_evidence.craft: The day, time, title and badge fit without awkward wrapping. The focus ring frames both cells after booking.
rating_evidence.usability: One keyboard action changes the available ticket into a compact booked record with its complete schedule visible.

primary_action.input: Tab to the full-width “Reserve shift” button, then Enter.
primary_action.expected: Confirm exactly one Wednesday 4–6 pm Packing shift under Upcoming shifts.
primary_action.observed: The empty message and action row disappeared. One Packing article showed “Booked”, retained the day and time, and received visible keyboard focus.

2B-390.edge_observation: A second Enter left one record. Reload returned the shift to Available. I reserved it again and verified one booked article.
2B-390.weakness: Initially, “No shifts scheduled” sits immediately above a dated shift. The small Available pill carries most of the distinction between the schedule and the offer.
2B-390.repair: Place a visible “Available shift” label above the ticket and remove it when the booking moves into Upcoming shifts.
2B-390.strength: The phone layout preserves the two details a volunteer needs to compare first: when the shift runs and what the work is.

1.reason: A gives the actual tool visual priority and uses the pegboard to explain both the missing item and its available alternative at both widths. B handles clearing better and keeps the field ready for editing.

2.reason: A leads narrowly. Its visible “Available shift” label and recognizable parcel card make the move from offer to booking easier to follow across both sizes. B presents the time more clearly and has the better post-booking focus target.

scope: Two original empty-state briefs, freshly matched live. Diagnostic anchors and one critic round.
